reference.source: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry; DSM-5-TR
clinicalPearls: Occurs on reduction or cessation of heavy, sustained alcohol use, with symptoms typically emerging within hours to a few days
Early features include tremor, anxiety, agitation, sweating, nausea, tachycardia, and hypertension; insomnia and irritability are common
Withdrawal seizures (typically generalised tonic-clonic) tend to occur early, usually within the first day or two
Alcoholic hallucinosis produces hallucinations, often visual, with an otherwise clear sensorium, distinguishing it from delirium tremens
Delirium tremens is a later, life-threatening complication with clouded consciousness, disorientation, severe autonomic hyperactivity, and hallucinations, usually appearing after a couple of days
Management principles rest on benzodiazepine-based regimens, often symptom-triggered using a standardised withdrawal scale, in a supportive monitored setting
Give thiamine before or with glucose to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy, and correct fluid and electrolyte disturbances
Assess withdrawal severity and complication risk with a validated instrument and identify high-risk patients for closer monitoring
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic alcohol exposure enhances inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric acid signalling and suppresses excitatory glutamatergic (NMDA receptor) activity; the brain adapts by downregulating GABA and upregulating glutamate systems. When alcohol is withdrawn, this adaptation leaves a state of central nervous system hyperexcitability and autonomic overactivity, producing the tremor, seizures, and delirium of the withdrawal syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Delirium from other causes (infection, metabolic derangement)
Sepsis or central nervous system infection
additionalInvestigations: Validated withdrawal severity scale to guide symptom-triggered treatment
Electrolytes including magnesium and phosphate, glucose, and renal function
Liver function tests and full blood count
Assessment for infection and other precipitants of delirium
Thiamine status and evaluation for Wernicke encephalopathy
redFlags: Delirium tremens with severe autonomic instability, a medical emergency with appreciable mortality if untreated
Signs of Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia)
Hyperthermia, marked tachycardia, and haemodynamic instability
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated withdrawal usually resolves within several days with appropriate treatment. Delirium tremens carries significant mortality if unrecognised but is greatly reduced with timely benzodiazepine therapy and supportive care. Long-term prognosis depends on engagement with relapse prevention and treatment of alcohol use disorder.
pitfalls: Giving glucose before thiamine and precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
Underestimating severity and under-dosing benzodiazepines in early withdrawal
Attributing agitation solely to withdrawal while missing infection, bleeding, or metabolic causes
Failing to identify patients at high risk of seizures or delirium tremens
Not addressing underlying alcohol use disorder after acute treatment
management: Benzodiazepine-based therapy such as chlordiazepoxide, diazepam or lorazepam, often symptom-triggered using a validated withdrawal scale
Parenteral thiamine given before glucose to prevent and treat Wernicke encephalopathy
Correct fluid and electrolyte deficits including magnesium, phosphate and potassium
Supportive care in a calm, monitored environment with attention to hydration and orientation
Treat delirium tremens promptly with escalating benzodiazepines, adjunctive antipsychotics for agitation and hallucinations, and critical care support
Identify and treat precipitants and comorbidities such as infection, injury or gastrointestinal haemorrhage
Link to relapse-prevention and specialist addiction services once acute withdrawal resolves
